# **Detecting Aimbot Usage in Minecraft Using a Long Short-Term** **Memory Model**

The gaming industry has long been at the cutting edge of technology, sometimes at the cost of proper game security. This has lead to an industry of cheaters, in particular among online video games. The ability to catch cheaters is of interest to game server operators who want to maintain integrity and trust with their player-base. A form of cheating that is particularly problematic is the use of aiming robots (aimbots) that use client-side hacks to lock onto targets and perform maximum damage. Aimbots are common in first-person style player-vs-player type video games where they have the most potential to give the cheater a significant unfair advantage. Minecraft, for example, is a game that has a large online player base who enjoy player-vs-player combat mini-games. Hacked clients are readily available to the average player and thus there is a strong need to be able to detect this cheating behaviour on the server side. Significant consideration toward fairness must be given to any solution that attempts to detect behaviour that would result in disciplinary action. Thus, it is important to maintain very high levels of accuracy as to avoid the false flagging of players who did not cheat. Further, any system that does not detect true aimbotters with very high accuracy would undermine player trust in the system. Therefore, we propose in this paper, a neural network approach to aimbot detection using Long Short-Term Memory to classify cheaters based on their movements over time. Our network achieves very high accuracy at high confidence levels, providing a notable improvement over a Gated Recurrent Network on the same data. We believe the network at these accuracy levels could have significant practical use in real-world servers.

Historically the video game industry has stayed at the cutting edge of technology, sometimes at the cost of implementing proper security features [1]. This gives many would-be hackers an easier time when trying to find exploits in games. This is a smaller problem in single player games since the exploits would not affect other players directly. However, in the online gaming sphere the poor security of a game may allow hackers to leverage exploits to their own advantage. Though there are a wide range of exploit categories, one of particular interest is cheating through misplaced trust. This is the act of tampering on the client-side with the game code, configuration data, or both, allowing one to take advantage of the trust put in the client [2]. A cheater can tamper with their client’s game states directly in a way that would not otherwise be possible for players [2]. A specific example of this kind of exploit would be the automatic aiming robot, also known as an aimbot. Aimbots use the internal game state of the client to lock the player’s camera perfectly onto the target without any human intervention. This specific form of exploitation is seen often in first-person combat games, where the accuracy of one’s mouse movements and click timings is critical. Many players enjoy playing the game in its multiplayer mode. Multiplayer experiences come in the form of individual servers that are hosted by third-parties. Some of these servers have massive player bases. For example, Hypixel is an incredibly popular server that garners tens of thousands of unique players online per day [4]. The server hosts many player-vs-player (PvP) based competitive minigames in which different players fight eachother to win. There is a lot of skill involved in PvP combat. Players must be strategic, have fast reflexes, maintain accuracy, and perform well-timed mouse clicks. As many players compete to climb server leaderboards, this leads some to pursue in-game cheating to gain a competitive advantage. A community of cheaters has risen in the Minecraft scene, creating open source clients such as LiquidBounce [5] to provide a whole host of cheating utilities to the masses. One of the offerings of the LiquidBounce client is an aimbot that locks onto targets and simulates mouse clicks that are perfectly timed to inflict maximum damage in combat. It is clear to see that a third-party who is hosting a server would have an incentive to reduce cheating in their servers to boost player retention rates. Thus, the highly accurate detection of such aimbots is important to maintain player trust. Our paper starts with a background of different approaches to the aimbot detection problem. Next, we introduce a neural network approach to aimbot detection, utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) as the primary architecture block to identify aimbot patterns from movement data. Then taking inspiration from literature [6], we adopted their proposed Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) architecture, tailoring it to our use case, allowing us to demonstrate the benefits of LSTM on long-sequence data. We then discuss our results and compare them to the performance of similar aimbot detectors. We also investigate the viability of our model in a live setting. The dataset used for our study comes from Kaggle and contains two large tables of time series data [12]. One table is the raw aiming information captured from a Minecraft user who does not have an aimbot enabled and the other table is the raw aiming information from a user who does have an aimbot enabled [12]. The author of the dataset calls these the legit and cheater tables, respectively [12]. The data is sorted by groups of unique IDs that appear to correspond to different sessions, as the same unique IDs are present in both the cheater and legit tables. Within each table we have access to fifteen features. The `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch` features describe the player’s camera rotations and their changes between samples. The `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z` features indicate where the player’s camera is looking. The `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` features specify the player’s coordinates. The `sensitivity` feature is the player’s camera sensitivity. The `time` feature in the milliseconds since Unix Epoch format captures when the sample was taken. Lastly, the `new_sequence` feature is set to true when a new movement sequence has started, and is false when the sample is within a sequence. In many other first-person combat games, aiming behaviour may involve more nuanced details of what may serve to characterize a player of being in suspicion of aimbotting. For example, in a first-person shooter style game, usually more damage is dealt by hitting specific regions of the opponents’ hitbox. Thus, information about what areas are being hit may be critical in determining suspicious behaviour. Where-as in Minecraft, the location of a strike within combat is not relevant in the damage calculations. Rather, combat is generally very sporadic, involving significant clicking, and rapid mouse movements to try and track the player during their movements in close quarters. It is for this reason that we believe the features used for detection, being the movement, aiming, and positional information as detailed above, is sufficient to make accurate predictions about suspicious behaviour. As within a game like Minecraft, it would be highly unlikely that a player would exhibit any kind of lock-in-like behaviour on a target given the nature of its combat system. The first step to processing this data was splitting the tables into groups by unique ID. We then sorted the samples by the `time` column to ensure all the readings were in correct chronological order. Next, we cut the dataset into individual samples. We did this by utilizing the `new_sequence` column in the dataset, splitting a new data point at each new sequence. Next, we removed the `sensitivity`, `time`, and `new_sequence` columns from the data row as we believed that these features were not significant to whether someone was aimbotting or not. The rationale for this is that the user’s sensitivity does not affect their targeting behaviour, the time is simply affected by the sampling rate, and the new sequence is purely a measure of when the user started their movement, which we already used for splitting the samples. We then appended these individual samples to our processed dataset array and the target class label being either 0 if it was a legit sample or 1 if it was a cheater sample. We believed it to be most appropriate to split on each `new sequence` since in practice this would be a similar behaviour to what we imagined a server-side implementation would do. The authors of BotScreen, an RNN based aimbot detector, noted that RNNs generally expect sequences to exist in regular intervals [6]. Thus, they normalized their data into 16ms intervals via linear interpolation of the event data [6]. We did not need to take this approach in our paper, as the sampling rate of the data was naturally very consistent. As many of the features vary in scale, we performed z-score normalization. We found in our testing that this normalization resulted in better convergence during training when compared to no normalization.

chunks.raw_text: It is evident that by the nature of this problem being a time series, that some form of RNN was most applicable. We weighed the possible available options by consulting literature to explore approaches to similar problems. Common networks for time series data were Long Short-Term Memory and Gated Recurrent Unit networks as shown in Section 2. LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network that gives a solution to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem seen in traditional RNNs [13]. LSTM is known to be effective at capturing longterm temporal dependencies [14]. Further, they are very generalized and can handle many kinds of problems [14]. Gated Recurrent Unit networks are similar to LSTMs, however, they omit the output gate that controls the level to which its memory is exposed, and thus exposes the full state at each time step [15]. From empirical results in one study, it was not possible to determine whether LSTM or GRU was inherently a better kind of recurrent network [15]. Rather, it appeared as though the choice of which network performs better depends on the dataset [15]. Transformers were also not considered, since they are generally less suited towards time series data, especially when the series are long-term, as shown in a study where the authors compared Transformer models to LSTM models in a stock price time series task [16]. We hypothesized that an LSTM network would be best suited for the detection of aimbotting on our dataset’s features since the sequences are reasonably long and would thus benefit from the use of the output gate. To test our hypothesis we explored the use of both our own proposed LSTM network and a bidirectional GRU based network proposed in [6]. We slightly modified the model in [6] by switching the loss metric to binary cross entropy loss opposed to their use of mean squared error. This was done to support our desired binary outputs from the model. It follows therefore, that we also added a sigmoid activation on the output of the model. For the GRU based model we used all the other hyper-parameters detailed in [6], being, a 3 layer bidirectional GRU with 10% dropout, 64 hidden units per layer, and batch sizes of 64. Our proposed network architecture shown in Figure 2 consists of a four-layered LSTM block followed by a fully connected layer that connects the hidden states in the final layer of the LSTM to a single output neuron. For the first three layers of the LSTM we applied 30% dropout to help improve regularization of the network. We applied the sigmoid function to bind our output to (0, 1), effectively giving us a probability of whether the input data is an aimbot or not. The input to the network is a sequence of 35 consecutive movement samples from the player where each sample consists of 12 features, being: `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch`, `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z`, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` . During training, validation, and testing we used batch sizes of 128.

Where TruePositives are the number of samples correctly identified as aimbotting, and TrueNegatives are the number of samples correctly identified as non-aimbotting behaviour. Accuracy is a metric that evaluates which proportion of samples were identified correctly. For both binary classifier models, this is a meaningful metric as the output is either true or false with respect to whether the movement is indicative of aimbotting or not. Further, we care about accuracy being high, as false positives or false negatives means either a player is being flagged and potentially punished for an offense they did not commit, or the player committing the offense is not being caught at all. Thus, it is critical for the model to be usable in real-world applications in which the promotion of fairness is key, that it be able to maintain a high accuracy. To better understand the confidence of the model, we used seven accuracy threshold values that determine at which confidence level the model classifies the prediction as a true positive. These seven values are: 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, and 0.99. Where a high threshold represents a higher level of confidence required to classify the sample as aimbotting.

chunks.raw_text: It is clear that a server-side approach for aimbot detection is critical for Minecraft. With the game’s expansive modding community, any client-side logic would be easily defeated. A hacked client would simply remove any anti-cheat logic. Thus, for this aimbot detection system to be viable it must be integratable into a real Minecraft server. For the purposes of this study we briefly investigated a popular Minecraft server software. PaperMC is a fast and secure Minecraft server that also has a powerful plugin system for developers to add their own server functionality [18]. We must be able to use the plugin API to capture the player information needed to create equivalent time series to the ones used to train the model. The first required features `yaw, pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, and `accel_pitch` are obtainable via the functions `getBodyYaw` from the `LivingEntity` class and `getPitch` from the `Entity` class which are both parents to the `Player` class and thus inherited by it [19, 20]. The next three features `target_x`, `target_y`, and `target_z` are obtainable via the function `getTargetBlock` from the `LivingEntity` class which is a parent to the `Player` class and thus inherited by it [19, 20]. Lastly, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` are all obtainable via the `getLocation` function from the `Entity` class which is a parent to the `Player` class and thus inherited by it [19, 21]. From our brief inspection of the plugin API, the information required to make use of our model in a live server is available.

# **Detecting Aimbot Usage in Minecraft Using a Long Short-Term** **Memory Model**

The gaming industry has long been at the cutting edge of technology, sometimes at the cost of proper game security. This has lead to an industry of cheaters, in particular among online video games. The ability to catch cheaters is of interest to game server operators who want to maintain integrity and trust with their player-base. A form of cheating that is particularly problematic is the use of aiming robots (aimbots) that use client-side hacks to lock onto targets and perform maximum damage. Aimbots are common in first-person style player-vs-player type video games where they have the most potential to give the cheater a significant unfair advantage. Minecraft, for example, is a game that has a large online player base who enjoy player-vs-player combat mini-games. Hacked clients are readily available to the average player and thus there is a strong need to be able to detect this cheating behaviour on the server side. Significant consideration toward fairness must be given to any solution that attempts to detect behaviour that would result in disciplinary action. Thus, it is important to maintain very high levels of accuracy as to avoid the false flagging of players who did not cheat. Further, any system that does not detect true aimbotters with very high accuracy would undermine player trust in the system. Therefore, we propose in this paper, a neural network approach to aimbot detection using Long Short-Term Memory to classify cheaters based on their movements over time. Our network achieves very high accuracy at high confidence levels, providing a notable improvement over a Gated Recurrent Network on the same data. We believe the network at these accuracy levels could have significant practical use in real-world servers.

The idea was that since the RNN was only trained on benign movements, any movements from an aimbot would provide worse RNN predictions (higher anomaly score) as it deviates from the behaviour of the benign movements [6]. The data is sorted by groups of unique IDs that appear to correspond to different sessions, as the same unique IDs are present in both the cheater and legit tables. Within each table we have access to fifteen features. The `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch` features describe the player’s camera rotations and their changes between samples. The `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z` features indicate where the player’s camera is looking. The `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` features specify the player’s coordinates. The `sensitivity` feature is the player’s camera sensitivity. The `time` feature in the milliseconds since Unix Epoch format captures when the sample was taken. Lastly, the `new_sequence` feature is set to true when a new movement sequence has started, and is false when the sample is within a sequence. In many other first-person combat games, aiming behaviour may involve more nuanced details of what may serve to characterize a player of being in suspicion of aimbotting. For example, in a first-person shooter style game, usually more damage is dealt by hitting specific regions of the opponents’ hitbox. Thus, information about what areas are being hit may be critical in determining suspicious behaviour. Where-as in Minecraft, the location of a strike within combat is not relevant in the damage calculations. Rather, combat is generally very sporadic, involving significant clicking, and rapid mouse movements to try and track the player during their movements in close quarters. It is for this reason that we believe the features used for detection, being the movement, aiming, and positional information as detailed above, is sufficient to make accurate predictions about suspicious behaviour. As within a game like Minecraft, it would be highly unlikely that a player would exhibit any kind of lock-in-like behaviour on a target given the nature of its combat system. The first step to processing this data was splitting the tables into groups by unique ID. We then sorted the samples by the `time` column to ensure all the readings were in correct chronological order. Next, we cut the dataset into individual samples. We did this by utilizing the `new_sequence` column in the dataset, splitting a new data point at each new sequence. Next, we removed the `sensitivity`, `time`, and `new_sequence` columns from the data row as we believed that these features were not significant to whether someone was aimbotting or not. The rationale for this is that the user’s sensitivity does not affect their targeting behaviour, the time is simply affected by the sampling rate, and the new sequence is purely a measure of when the user started their movement, which we already used for splitting the samples. We then appended these individual samples to our processed dataset array and the target class label being either 0 if it was a legit sample or 1 if it was a cheater sample. We believed it to be most appropriate to split on each `new sequence` since in practice this would be a similar behaviour to what we imagined a server-side implementation would do. The authors of BotScreen, an RNN based aimbot detector, noted that RNNs generally expect sequences to exist in regular intervals [6]. Thus, they normalized their data into 16ms intervals via linear interpolation of the event data [6]. We did not need to take this approach in our paper, as the sampling rate of the data was naturally very consistent. As many of the features vary in scale, we performed z-score normalization. We found in our testing that this normalization resulted in better convergence during training when compared to no normalization.

chunks.raw_text: It is evident that by the nature of this problem being a time series, that some form of RNN was most applicable. We weighed the possible available options by consulting literature to explore approaches to similar problems. Common networks for time series data were Long Short-Term Memory and Gated Recurrent Unit networks as shown in Section 2. LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network that gives a solution to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem seen in traditional RNNs [13]. LSTM is known to be effective at capturing longterm temporal dependencies [14]. Further, they are very generalized and can handle many kinds of problems [14]. Gated Recurrent Unit networks are similar to LSTMs, however, they omit the output gate that controls the level to which its memory is exposed, and thus exposes the full state at each time step [15]. From empirical results in one study, it was not possible to determine whether LSTM or GRU was inherently a better kind of recurrent network [15]. Rather, it appeared as though the choice of which network performs better depends on the dataset [15]. Transformers were also not considered, since they are generally less suited towards time series data, especially when the series are long-term, as shown in a study where the authors compared Transformer models to LSTM models in a stock price time series task [16]. We hypothesized that an LSTM network would be best suited for the detection of aimbotting on our dataset’s features since the sequences are reasonably long and would thus benefit from the use of the output gate. To test our hypothesis we explored the use of both our own proposed LSTM network and a bidirectional GRU based network proposed in [6]. We slightly modified the model in [6] by switching the loss metric to binary cross entropy loss opposed to their use of mean squared error. This was done to support our desired binary outputs from the model. It follows therefore, that we also added a sigmoid activation on the output of the model. For the GRU based model we used all the other hyper-parameters detailed in [6], being, a 3 layer bidirectional GRU with 10% dropout, 64 hidden units per layer, and batch sizes of 64. Our proposed network architecture shown in Figure 2 consists of a four-layered LSTM block followed by a fully connected layer that connects the hidden states in the final layer of the LSTM to a single output neuron. For the first three layers of the LSTM we applied 30% dropout to help improve regularization of the network. We applied the sigmoid function to bind our output to (0, 1), effectively giving us a probability of whether the input data is an aimbot or not. The input to the network is a sequence of 35 consecutive movement samples from the player where each sample consists of 12 features, being: `yaw`, `pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, `accel_pitch`, `target_x`, `target_y`, `target_z`, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` . During training, validation, and testing we used batch sizes of 128.

Where TruePositives are the number of samples correctly identified as aimbotting, and TrueNegatives are the number of samples correctly identified as non-aimbotting behaviour. Accuracy is a metric that evaluates which proportion of samples were identified correctly. For both binary classifier models, this is a meaningful metric as the output is either true or false with respect to whether the movement is indicative of aimbotting or not. Further, we care about accuracy being high, as false positives or false negatives means either a player is being flagged and potentially punished for an offense they did not commit, or the player committing the offense is not being caught at all. Thus, it is critical for the model to be usable in real-world applications in which the promotion of fairness is key, that it be able to maintain a high accuracy. To better understand the confidence of the model, we used seven accuracy threshold values that determine at which confidence level the model classifies the prediction as a true positive. It is clear that a server-side approach for aimbot detection is critical for Minecraft. With the game’s expansive modding community, any client-side logic would be easily defeated. A hacked client would simply remove any anti-cheat logic. Thus, for this aimbot detection system to be viable it must be integratable into a real Minecraft server. For the purposes of this study we briefly investigated a popular Minecraft server software. PaperMC is a fast and secure Minecraft server that also has a powerful plugin system for developers to add their own server functionality [18]. We must be able to use the plugin API to capture the player information needed to create equivalent time series to the ones used to train the model. The first required features `yaw, pitch`, `delta_yaw`, `delta_pitch`, `accel_yaw`, and `accel_pitch` are obtainable via the functions `getBodyYaw` from the `LivingEntity` class and `getPitch` from the `Entity` class which are both parents to the `Player` class and thus inherited by it [19, 20]. The next three features `target_x`, `target_y`, and `target_z` are obtainable via the function `getTargetBlock` from the `LivingEntity` class which is a parent to the `Player` class and thus inherited by it [19, 20]. Lastly, `position_x`, `position_y`, and `position_z` are all obtainable via the `getLocation` function from the `Entity` class which is a parent to the `Player` class and thus inherited by it [19, 21]. From our brief inspection of the plugin API, the information required to make use of our model in a live server is available.

We used the bidirectional GRU network on our dataset to provide our LSTM model a comparison to current literature.
